Copyright and trade-secret law protect legitimate interests. A manufacturer should not have to publish source code merely because a technician needs a wiring diagram. Instructions for diagnosing a product, safely replacing a component, and restoring ordinary operation are functional repair inputs. A control module may require a serial number, cryptographic handshake, or software authorization before accepting a replacement. Pairing can serve real purposes, including safety and theft prevention. It can also become a gate that independent shops can’t open, even when they’re installing a lawful part for the product’s owner.

# A manual is a tool

A repair manual is not a decorative extra. It is a tool, as necessary to modern repair as a multimeter or lift. Yet manufacturers increasingly treat service information (manuals, diagrams, software procedures, and fault definitions) as intellectual property that can be withheld, delayed, or placed behind restrictive subscriptions. The machine may belong to the customer, but the knowledge required to fix it remains under someone else’s control—that hidden condition can turn ownership into dependency.

Copyright and trade-secret law protect legitimate interests. A manufacturer should not have to publish source code merely because a technician needs a wiring diagram. But service information does not become commercially untouchable simply because a company compiled it. Instructions for diagnosing a product, safely replacing a component, and restoring ordinary operation are functional repair inputs. Calling those inputs “proprietary” doesn’t answer the public-interest question. It only changes the label on the locked door.

For a small shop, missing information has immediate costs. A technician may spend hours reconstructing a diagnostic sequence that the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) has already documented. A vehicle can occupy a bay while the shop searches for diagnostic trouble codes (DTCs), connector locations, torque specifications, or calibration steps. The customer waits, labor becomes harder to quote, and a routine repair may be sent to an authorized network—not because that network has better tools, but because it received the instructions.

What happens when the replacement part is available, affordable, and physically correct, but the product refuses to recognize it? That is where documentation and parts pairing meet. A control module may require a serial number, cryptographic handshake, or software authorization before accepting a replacement. Pairing can serve real purposes, including safety and theft prevention. It can also become a gate that independent shops can’t open, even when they’re installing a lawful part for the product’s owner.

Without documentation, a shop cannot reliably distinguish a genuine safety requirement from an artificial restriction. Without access to the pairing procedure, the manual is incomplete—the instructions lead directly to a wall. And without the identifiers needed to complete that procedure (a sensor code, calibration file, or authorization token), the replacement part is little more than an expensive paperweight. The technical manual and the digital permission system are therefore one repair infrastructure, not separate policy questions.

The cost spreads beyond a single invoice. Independent shops must either buy overlapping subscriptions, invest unpaid time in reverse engineering, decline work, or accept dependence on a competitor. Customers may lose local options and face longer trips or delays. Reusable parts can’t return to service when pairing blocks their installation, which may increase waste. The market still appears to offer parts and repair businesses, but the practical route between them has been cut—like publishing a card catalog while locking the library stacks.

A practical disclosure rule should require manufacturers to provide independent repair providers and product owners with the same service information available to authorized technicians (independent and authorized alike), at the same time and in a usable electronic format. That information should include manuals, schematics, diagnostic data, error-code definitions, required software, pairing procedures, calibration instructions, and necessary credentials. Access may carry a reasonable cost, but it should not be priced or licensed to defeat independent use. Updates should remain available for the product’s supported life, and corrections should be published promptly.

The rule also needs a narrow exception for material that would reveal unrelated source code or create a specific, demonstrable security risk. A manufacturer invoking that exception should identify the withheld material and explain why a less restrictive disclosure cannot address the risk. “Intellectual property” should not function as a universal password—especially when the withheld information is already given to selected repairers. Regulators should be able to order disclosure, penalize delay, and prevent contract terms from stripping away the rule.

We should judge repair policy by whether a capable shop can complete a lawful repair, not by whether a manufacturer technically offers a manual somewhere. Put the manual, the pairing process, and the required credentials on equal terms. If lawmakers want a competitive repair market, our rule must be simple: when a product can be repaired, the information needed to repair it must be available.
